title: Candy Corn Bag

drivers.name: price increase (6.0% vs regular)
drivers.evidence: Recent weeks with same price (4.08) and no promotion: 13 units (2026-09-28) and 3 units (2026-10-05), both below baseline. Noise-adjusted effect of price hikes is x0.75. Two consistent observations.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 10.3. The price is raised 6.0% above regular (3.85 → 4.08), and this week has no event or promotion. Past promotions at similar price points show median lift x2.15, but noise-adjusted lift is only x1.45. However, the most recent price increase (2026-09-28) saw sales drop to 13 units (vs baseline 10.3), with no promotion—indicating price sensitivity. The 2026-10-05 week (same price, no event) sold only 3 units, confirming downward pressure. The classical model suggests no lift, but judgment overrides: price increase likely suppresses demand. A price hike of this size with no promotion or event should reduce sales. Noise-adjusted effect of price increases is x0.75 (from 2026-09-28 and 2026-10-05). Evidence is strong (2 recent data points). No seasonal or event driver. Adjust down.

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 4.08 (+6.0% vs regular price 3.85)

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 10.3 | 5%-95%: 0.0 - 24.6 | 10%-90%: 0.0 - 19.2

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-85% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
